content: Darwin's tubercle is a congenital condition of the ear that manifests as a thickened nodule on the helix, specifically at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the ear. This anatomical feature is present in approximately 4% of the population. The nodule, which is pointed or acuminate in shape, is thought to represent a vestigial remnant of the mammalian ear structure. This feature is considered atavistic, meaning it is a throwback to ancestral traits, and it was first described by Charles Darwin in the opening pages of his work The Descent of Man. Darwin presented it as evidence of a vestigial structure, supporting the concept of common ancestry among primates. Interestingly, Darwin himself referred to it as the Woolnerian tip, naming it after Thomas Woolner, a British sculptor who had depicted this feature in one of his sculptures and was the first to theorize its atavistic nature. The genetic basis for Darwin's tubercle is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. However, the gene exhibits variable penetrance, meaning that not all individuals who carry the gene will necessarily express the physical manifestation of the ear tubercle.
